body.heading: A year that is not quite 365 days
paragraphs: A calendar has an awkward job: fit whole days into a year that refuses to be whole. Earth takes about 365 days, 5 hours and 49 minutes to circle the Sun. Julius Caesar's calendar, from 45 BC, rounded this to 365 days plus one leap day every four years — close, but about eleven minutes too generous each year.

Eleven minutes sounds like nothing. But minutes compound: after sixteen centuries, the calendar had drifted ten full days, and the spring equinox — used to set the date of Easter — was falling on 11 March instead of 21 March.

body.heading: The great skip
paragraphs: Pope Gregory XIII's reform of 1582 made two fixes. First, the skip: in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Poland, Thursday 4 October was followed directly by Friday 15 October. Rent, wages and birthdays caused predictable grumbling, but the sky and the calendar agreed again.

Second, a smarter leap rule: century years are leap years only if divisible by 400. So 2000 was a leap year, but 1700, 1800 and 1900 were not. The Gregorian calendar now drifts by only about a day every 3,000 years.

body.heading: Adoption, slowly and suspiciously
paragraphs: Not everyone trusted a pope's arithmetic. Britain and its colonies waited until 1752, by which time they had to skip eleven days; Russia held out until 1918, and Greece until 1923. Travellers of the era sometimes crossed a border and changed date by nearly a fortnight.
Today the Gregorian calendar is the world's shared civil calendar — a quiet piece of international agreement, maintained by nothing more than everyone continuing to use it.

takeaway: The Gregorian reform skipped ten days in 1582 and refined the leap year, fixing an eleven-minute yearly error that had grown for 1,600 years.
